name: Collar stays

lead: Collar stays are thin rigid strips slipped into pockets under the points of a dress shirt collar to keep them flat and sharp.
They are used for a crisp neckline. No scholarly evidence exists; it is a tailoring convention.

paras: The stiff strip prevents the collar tip from curling or bending.
Plastic stays can warp or break and should be removed before laundry or ironing; metal stays last longer. Benefits are small and temporary.

lead: A collar stay is a smooth strip of rigid material, rounded at one end and pointed at the other, that slides into a pocket on the underside of a dress-shirt collar to keep the collar points stable. Wikipedia says the stays help the collar lie flat against the collarbone and stay crisp and correctly placed.[1] They go by several names, including collar stiffener, collar stick and, in British English, collar bone or collar tab.[1]

Stays are made of plastic, metal such as brass, stainless steel or sterling silver, horn, baleen or mother of pearl.[1] Shirts commonly ship with plastic stays that can bend, and metal replacements are sold to avoid that.[1] No scientific studies of collar stays were found; the topic is covered by reference descriptions of the accessory and by tailoring convention.[1][2]
infobox: Plastic, brass, stainless steel, sterling silver, horn, baleen, mother of pearl [1]

paras: Stays are manufactured in several lengths for different collar designs, and some are adjustable in length.[1] Grokipedia gives typical dimensions of two to three inches in length and about nine millimetres in width, and distinguishes removable stays from permanently sewn-in versions.[2] Wikipedia notes that some shirts use shorter, wider stays than the classic form, which the classic stay will not fit.[1]

Variations include metal stays sold with magnets that hold the collar against the shirt, stays with a small button hook at one end to help fasten tiny buttons, and adhesive stays that stiffen the collar or attach the points to the shirt.[1] Grokipedia reports magnetic stays from brands such as Wurkin Stiffs from around 2015.[2]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, places the origin of collar stays in the early twentieth century as an alternative to heavily starched detachable collars, saying they were introduced around 1908 as collar supporters and that earlier supports used materials like bone or wood. It describes a shift to plastic stays after World War II, including a 1953 patent attributed to Andrew Doric Charles for a thin pointed tab, and standardisation in mass-produced dress shirts in the 1950s to 1970s.[2] These dates have not been verified against primary sources here.

The stiff strip resists the bending and curling of the collar tip, holding the points in a flat, defined line. Sources describe this as framing the neck and face more neatly, especially under a jacket or with a tie, and supporting a stable tie knot.[2]

The effect is small and tied to wearing the shirt. No controlled studies measure whether crisp collar points change how a wearer is perceived, so claims about their visual value come from tailoring convention and style writing rather than from research.

Wikipedia reports that stays are removed before dry cleaning or pressing, because cleaning can damage both shirt and stay, and that pressing a collar with the stays in can leave an impression of the stay in the fabric. Plastic stays may need replacing if they bend, and some shirts have stays sewn in that cannot be removed.[1] There are no medical risks associated with the accessory.

In style-focused communities, metal stays are mentioned as a minor upgrade to dress shirts, and the wiki's summary says crisp collars frame the face. This is a community characterisation about presentation; it has not been tested.

Reference descriptions indicate that stays are sold at haberdashers, sewing-supply shops and men's clothing stores, in multiple lengths and materials, and that metal stays are less prone to bending than plastic ones.[1]

timeline.event: Collar stays are introduced as collar supporters, according to Grokipedia.[2]
A patent for a thin pointed plastic stay is granted, according to Grokipedia.[2]
